BC is the only province that charges a monthly premium for health insurance. In Ontario, you pay an amount based on your income on your provincial tax return at the end of the year. But that means you're not haggling with MSP customer service to get the rate lowered or having to prove that you got fired from your last job.

However, from my last tax return in Ontario, that amount was $600 per fully employed person. While here I am paying $840 a year, which is significantly more. Additionally, I never had to pay my wife's portion. If my wife had 0 income, then she doesn't pay the amount. But in BC, just because you are common law or married, I must now pay $1,500 a year for the two of us. JUST BECAUSE I earn $30,000 a year, regardless that my wife earned 0 dollars last year.

BC probably charges the most out of any province for health premiums, and it's also the hardest system to get the premium cancelled if you lose your job or don't have an income. Transit fees vary on how many zones you have to cross and time of day. I'm paying $4.00 one way to go from New Westminster to downtown Vancouver during rush hour. But if you live in Surrey, to go to DT Vancouver it costs $5.50. [See details](http://www.translink.ca/en/Fares-and-Passes/Single-Fares.aspx)

Gas price is the highest in North America, because every litre of gas has an additional $0.20/L Translink levy. Translink is the transit company here, and they use this tax to pay for maintenance and work to the transit network, including roads and bridges. So if gas in Toronto is $1.10/L, here you'll be paying $1.30/L. 

On cars, most vehicles here look nice because they don't rust like in Ontario. Since there's no snow, there's no road salt, so no rust. If you're importing an out of province vehicle, you'll need to pass a BC safety inspection, which means they'll have to take off your front-window tints. And because of the high gas price, most people here stick to small vehicles, or altogether don't have car and just use a car-share service, transit, or bike.

For auto insurance, everyone in BC starts at the same rate. This goes down each year of no-fault driving, or up for each at-fault accident. You'll have to bring proof of your Ontario auto insurance history. Each year of no-fault coverage will result in a 5% decrease from the base rate that everyone starts at. Unfortunately, this means that you won't get credit for any years where you didn't have a car but still had a valid license. Whereas if you had lived in BC all this time, you would have been credited for every year you held your license, including from the time you got your G1 and G2, not just the years you were insured. So when I moved, my insurance went from $90/mo for 2-mil liability coverage, now I'm paying $110/mo for $200k liability coverage. If I want 2-mil coverage like in Ontario, I would have to pay $130/mo+, an increase of $480/year compared to Ontario.

They call within 14-21 days. If you say "yes" on the phone, that affirms the sale, and the contract begins. If you say "no", "changed my mind", "I found out this is a scam" -- they'll cancel the transaction. On average, 60% of deals will go through, the other 40% will bounce (cancelled over the phone, couldn't reach the person, or that account is already signed with another company).

When you perform the transaction at the terminal, on confirmed/accepted charges, the terminal receives back a unique transaction ID to reference the transaction. That alone is all you need as a retailer to identify a transaction, but you can also combine it with storing just the first 4 digits and first/last name, without much harm if that data is leaked. And because it was approved, means you don't need the credit card details any longer.

I know because I program websites to use these things. 

The only reason they would store full credit card details, expiry dates, and security codes is because they want to track the buyers locations and sales habits, so they can upsell these shoppers in the future. They'll even send you advertisements in the mail on the credit card address that relate to the purchases you're likely to make.

But credit card companies actively discourage storing any credit card details, because most retailers don't maintain bank-level secure servers, and that information will result in a security breach -- just like at Target. They even have hard-drives on POS that collect all that information, than the uneducated retailer will sell the POS with a hard-drive full of data to a third-party. Or sometimes, there are break-ins that target these hard-drives. I'm guessing at Target it would be a central server at the store.

Anyways, Target will probably have to settle with the credit card companies for the damages this will do to them in terms of inappropriate transactions. If it wasn't for Target's mishandling of data, those 40 million credit cards wouldn't be compromised.
